content.title: What is a fire weather watch? NWS issues Florida alert
content.text: Dry air and gusty winds are setting the stage for elevated fire danger across parts of the Southeast heading into the weekend.A Fire Weather Watch has been issued by the National Weather Service for portions of the western Florida Panhandle, where conditions could allow fires to start easily and spread quickly.Here’s what the alert means, what could happen next and what residents are urged to do to reduce the risk.Is there a fire in Florida?There are no new active wildfires reported in Florida, but fire risk is increasing. The National Weather Service has issued a Fire Weather Watch for parts of the western Panhandle, where low humidity and gusty winds could allow any fires that develop to spread quickly. Forecasters say outdoor burning is not recommended.The danger comes as AccuWeather warns of increased wildfire risk across the Southeast and mid-Atlantic heading into spring, particularly in areas dealing with dry conditions."Early spring fire risk in the interior mid-Atlantic, southern Appalachians, and parts of the Southeast," the forecast states. "Drought concerns early, followed by increasing rain and flood risk along the Gulf Coast."AccuWeather spring 2026 forecast map shows elevated fire risks for the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic.What is a fire weather watch?A fire weather watch means conditions are favorable for dangerous wildfires to develop — but they are not happening yet.It is issued by the National Weather Service when a combination of factors could quickly lead to fire growth, including:Strong windsLow humidityDry vegetationThink of it as a heads-up: conditions could escalate into a red flag warning, which is more urgent.What is a red flag warning?A red flag warning means critical fire weather conditions are happening now or about to happen.Fires can start easily and spread rapidly — especially in open areas like the South Plains. This is when behavior matters most.Each NWS office creates local criteria for fire weather watches and red flag warnings.Florida wildfire mapWhat should you do during a red flag warning?Monitor local alertsStay updated with local wildfire offices, fire departments and emergency managementCheck air quality forecasts — smoke can reduce visibility and impact healthPrepare your home and propertyWater lawns, shrubs and trees if possibleClear dry brush, leaves and other flammable materialMove firewood, propane tanks and grills away from buildingsHave an emergency kit readyWater, non-perishable food, medicationsMasks (for smoke), flashlights, batteriesImportant documents and a first-aid kitKeep vehicles fueled in case of evacuationWhat not to during a red flag warning or fire weather watchAvoid anything that could spark a fireDo not burn trash or brushAvoid open flamesUse grills only on gravel or pavementDo not drive or park over dry grassMake sure chains or metal aren’t dragging from vehiclesBe careful with cigarettes, matches and even glass bottlesIf burning is allowedCover burn barrels with a weighted metal lid (holes no larger than 3/4 inch)Keep a 10-foot clear space around any fireFully extinguish with water — stir until colNever leave fires unattendedElectrical and safety hazardsReport downed utility poles or lines immediatelyStay away from anything that could be energizedHealth precautionsStay indoors if smoke increasesUse a mask or respirator if outsideFlorida weather watches and warningsStay informed. Get weather alerts via textBrandi D. Addison covers weather across the United States as the Weather Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network. She can be reached at baddison@gannett.com.
